get.summary: Every year the ledger covers, side by side.
get.description:
The year-on-year screen answers "what changed since last year". This answers
the question a decade of history makes possible and that one cannot: what a
category has been doing all along — rent climbing from 400 to 1.100, a car
bought in one January and never again, a subscription nobody cancelled.

Three things it must not do, all of them ways a long series lies:

* a year with no bookings is absent, not a zero — this ledger starts in
  November 2014, and drawing 2014 as a full year beside 2015 would say the year
  was frugal when ten months of it are simply not here. `months_per_year`
  travels with every figure so the caller can say so;
* a category with no activity in one year is a zero WITHIN its row, because a
  hole in the middle of a time series reads as missing data;
* nothing is averaged per year here. An average over a part year is the same
  lie one level down, and the caller has the month counts to do it honestly.

get.summary:
First-run bootstrap. Re-checks the user count inside the transaction, so two
concurrent setup requests cannot both create an admin.
Confirms a draft booking, optionally correcting its amount.
get.description:
A separate endpoint rather than a `status` field on `PUT /bookings/{id}`, for two
reasons. The PUT body is a full `BookingInput`, so a status field there would
travel on every ordinary edit and any client that forgot to echo it back would
silently re-draft — or silently confirm — a booking; and draft→confirmed is the
one transition that moves money into every total, so it deserves a request that
cannot be made by accident.

Correcting the amount belongs here because it is the entire reason the draft
exists: an `amountIsEstimate` template books 29,00 and the real invoice says
34,50. Confirming twice is harmless — the second call finds it already confirmed
and changes nothing else.

get.summary: Everything matching a phrase, across every year at once.
get.description:
The listing is deliberately year-scoped — a ledger is read a year at a time —
which makes "what have I ever paid this merchant" four page loads and a mental
addition. This answers it in one request, and the per-year summary IS the
answer: the matching rows are only the evidence for it.

Matching is case-insensitive on the trimmed comment, the same rule the category
rules use, so `Kaufland` and `kaufland` are one merchant and not two. It is a
CONTAINS match rather than the rule table's exact one, because a person
searching types a fragment where a rule states a whole key.

get.summary:
The tax report, whose running number ends up on a printed list handed to a tax
office — so the ordering has to be a function of the DATA, not of storage.
get.description:
`created_at` defaults to `now()`, which inside a transaction is the transaction's
timestamp: every row of one import commit carries the identical value, so it
breaks no ties at all. That left `b.id` — a random uuid — as the real tiebreaker,
which made `Nr.` arbitrary within a month and reshuffled it on any re-import.
`comment, amount_cents` restore determinism from the booking's own content; `id`
stays last only to keep the sort total for genuinely identical rows.

get.summary: Rebuilds an account from an export document.
get.description:
**Refuses a target that already has bookings.** Merge semantics for two ledgers
that both claim to be the truth would be an invention — which booking wins, what
happens to a rule that maps the same comment elsewhere — and inventing it quietly
is how money goes missing. This is a restore, not a sync.

Categories, rules and templates are matched by NAME, because ids are per-user: a
restore into a different account has to resolve them by the only thing both
accounts agree on.

post.summary: Re-scores every open suggestion against the bookings as they stand now.
post.description:
Suggestions are a statement about TWO ledgers, but they were only ever computed
when one of them moved — written when an expense is pulled, rewritten only when
that expense changes upstream. Import a year of bookings afterwards and every
existing draft keeps the empty candidate list it was born with. That is not
hypothetical: the drafts here were written at 20:51 and the bookings arrived at
20:58, so 459 suggestions had been scored against an empty ledger and nothing
ever asked them again.

get.summary: Readiness

Deleting a template leaves the bookings it already produced alone —
`bookings.template_id` is `ON DELETE SET NULL`. Money that has been spent does not
disappear because the plan for it was cancelled.

200.description: Vorlagen mit Fälligkeit im gefragten Monat

post.summary: Creates the bookings due in one month.
post.description:
The guard against double-booking is `ON CONFLICT ... DO NOTHING` on the partial
unique index. **The index predicate has to be repeated in the conflict target** —
without `WHERE template_id IS NOT NULL` Postgres cannot infer a partial index and
raises 42P10, which is exactly the trap the importer hit.

get.summary: The printable receipt list.
get.description:
Deliberately plain: A4, one table, a running number that matches the CSV and the
on-screen report, and a per-category summary at the end. The point is that it can
be printed, stapled to a folder of receipts and handed over — not that it is
pretty.

Text goes through printpdf's built-in Helvetica, which is WinAnsi-encoded.
Windows-1252 covers every German character including `ß`, `€` and the typographic
quotes; anything outside it is dropped by printpdf rather than substituted, which
is why the comment column is the user's own German data and not arbitrary input.

200.description: Steuerliste als CSV, Beträge deutsch formatiert

deltaCents.description: Current minus median: positive means it cost more than usual.

direction.description:
`above` or `below`, so the UI does not have to infer it from a sign it may
be displaying flipped.

items.description: Empty is the normal case and must render as nothing at all.

AuthChallenge.description: Drives the login page without the frontend knowing which provider is configured.

amountCents.description: Always positive; the direction is carried by `kind`.

bookedOn.description: Absent for imported history, which genuinely has no day.

categoryId.description:
`null` means no rule matched and no override was set. Never silently folded
into the real `Sonstiges` category.

counterparty.description:
Who the money was with, and what the bank wrote on the line. Both come from
a statement import and are `null` for everything else: they are what a bank
export knows and a hand-kept sheet never did.

monthName.description:
Server-rendered German month name. Always derivable, but including it removes
a client-side lookup from every list render.

netCents.description: `expense - income`, so a category that earned money nets negative.

categoryId.description: Sets a manual override. Omit to let the rule table decide.

sumIncomeCents.description: Sums for the CURRENT filter, so the UI never re-derives them client-side.

excludedTransferCount.description: Transfers are excluded from this analysis; the count lets the UI say so.

netIsNegative.description:
True when the category earned more than it cost. The UI must render this as a
credit, not as a bare negative cost.

shareOfTotal.description: Zero for negative-net categories — they have no share of the costs.

CompareRow.description:
One category, this year against last.

Every figure is in the stored expense-positive convention: a positive net is what
something cost, and a positive `deltaCents` means it cost MORE than last year (or,
for an income category, that less came in). The display flips that sign, exactly
as it does everywhere else.

comparableNetCents.description:
The same four figures over the months BOTH years actually have. This is the
pair that may be compared; the ones above are the full years as they stand.

deltaRatio.description:
`delta / |previous|`. `None` when there was nothing last year to be a share
of — a percentage against zero is not a large number, it is not a number.

isNew.description:
Nothing in this category last year, or nothing this year. Either makes the
percentage meaningless and both are worth saying out loud.

CompareTotals.description:
One year's headline figures, both as it stands and restricted to the months the
other year also has.

lastMonthWithData.description:
The last month of this year that holds a booking, or `None` for an empty
year. How far the year has actually got — which is where a trailing window
should end, and not something the client should have to infer.

monthsWithData.description:
Months carrying at least one booking. A nine-month year and a twelve-month
year are not comparable, and this is what says so.

CompareTypeRow.description: One category type, this year against last.

amountCents.description:
Confirming is also where an estimate's real amount is entered, because that
is the only reason the draft existed.

carryoverGapCents.description: Set when a configured opening disagrees with the previous year's close.

savingsDepositCents.description:
What was actually paid into the savings categories this year — the decision,
not the residue. This is what a person means by "meine Sparrate".

savingsDepositPerMonthCents.description: The same, per month with data, which is the form it is usually said in.

savingsDepositRate.description: Of real income, so it is comparable with `savingsRateConsumption`.

savingsRateNaive.description:
`balance / income` — reproduces the spreadsheet, and is misleading on its own
because gross income includes cost-sharing that is really negative expense.

importFingerprint.description:
Carried so a restore of an imported account stays idempotent against a later
re-import of the same workbook.

ExportDocument.description:
The full-export document.

Money here stays **integer cents**, because this file is the account's backup and
the input to `POST /exports/restore`. The CSV sibling is the one place de-DE
formatting is applied to exported money, and only because its reader is Excel.

Nothing references a uuid across the document except where it is internal to it:
categories, rules and templates are joined by NAME, because ids are per-user and
a restore into a different account must still resolve them.

formatVersion.description:
Bumped when the shape changes incompatibly; `restore` refuses what it cannot
read rather than guessing.

actualBalanceCents.description: Actual saldo so far — income minus expenses, so a gain is positive.

actualThroughMonth.description: The last month that holds bookings; `null` for a year with none.

dueTemplateCount.description:
How many templates fall due across the remaining months, counted once each
time they are due.

historyMonths.description: Months of history the medians were taken over.

method.description: Stated on the wire so the UI never has to guess what it is drawing.

projectedBalanceCents.description: The same for the projected months alone.

projectedFromMonth.description: The first projected month; `null` when the year is complete.

ForecastBasisRow.description:
One category's contribution to the projection, so the figure can be inspected
rather than believed.

source.description: `template`, `median` or `mixed` — where the figure came from.

closingBalanceCents.description: Running balance at the end of this month, projections included.

fixedCents.description:
The part the recurring templates account for. Zero in an actual month —
there the figure is what happened, not what was planned.

isProjected.description: The distinction that must survive into the UI.

monthName.description: German month name; data, not chrome.

netCents.description: Expense-positive, like every stored net: a cost is positive.

spreadCents.description:
Half-width of the range, from the median absolute deviation. Zero for an
actual month, which has no uncertainty left.

variableCents.description: What the medians add on top of the templates.

owedToTheFutureCents.description:
The headline: what these known lumps will still take out of the account this
year. The number the monthly saldo does not tell you.

FundStatus.description: One fund, measured against what has actually been spent this year.

accruedByMonthCents.description:
What should be aside by the end of the asked-about month. Proportional to the
ANNUAL amount, so twelve months come back to it exactly.

duePassed.description: Whether the due month is in the past relative to the asked-about month.

monthlyAccrualCents.description:
What to set aside each month. An approximation by construction — a year does
not always divide into twelve equal cents — which is why it is never the
figure the cumulative one is built from.

overUnderCents.description:
Accrued minus spent. Positive is a cushion; negative means the bill landed
before the fund had caught up with it.

remainingCents.description:
What is still expected to leave the account this year. Never negative: a bill
that came in cheaper does not become money owed to you.

spentCents.description: Net spending in the fund's category this year, stored sign: positive is cost.

FundSuggestion.description:
A fund the history argues for. Suggested, never created: the app does not get to
decide that a holiday is a recurring obligation.

monthsWithSpending.description:
How many months of the year the category was spent in at all. The point of
the suggestion is the clustering, so the evidence is returned with it.

markerTotalCents.description:
Sum of the legacy sheet's own month-end markers, which is the authoritative
carryover even where the rows disagree with it.

KoCategory.description:
A KitchenOwl expense category. A **different taxonomy** from the app's 32
categories: seven household labels with no relationship to Fixkosten/Variable
Kosten. Never auto-mapped, and the UI must not style it like an app category.

colorArgb.description: Packed ARGB as KitchenOwl stores it, not a CSS colour.

excludedCount.description:
Expenses KitchenOwl itself keeps out of its statistics, so this analysis
does too. Reported rather than hidden.

years.description:
The years the mirror holds anything for, newest first — the year picker
cannot borrow the personal ledger's years, which start earlier.

KoCategoryAnalysisRow.description:
One KitchenOwl category over a year.

Both figures, always: `amountCents` is what the household spent and
`ownShareCents` is the user's slice of it. They are different numbers with
different meanings and adding them is meaningless.

koCategoryId.description:
Null for expenses with no KitchenOwl category — the normal case for a third
of the live corpus, never an error.

shareOfTotal.description: Of the household's total, not of the user's share.

KoComparePayer.description: Who paid, this year against last.

KoCompareRow.description:
One KitchenOwl category, this year against last.

Both figures are carried through the comparison, and so are both deltas. A
household that spent 200 € more of which the user carries 100 € more is two
facts, and collapsing them to one would be the same mistake the single-year
view is built to avoid.

comparableAmountCents.description:
The same figures restricted to the months both years carry. The mirror
started on 2024-12-22, so 2024 against 2025 is a part year against a full
one and the raw totals would be a statement about the calendar.

deltaRatio.description:
`delta / previous`, absent when there is no previous to be a share of —
"+∞ %" for a category that did not exist last year is worse than nothing,
and `isNew` says what actually happened.

KoCompareTotals.description: One year's side of the comparison.

excludedCount.description: What KitchenOwl itself keeps out of its statistics, per year.

lastMonthWithData.description:
Where the year's data stops, so a trailing window can end there instead of
running into months that have not happened.

suggestedAction.description:
`link` when a candidate cleared the threshold, otherwise `none`. Never
`create`: a pull never writes a booking, and the 63-of-211 overlap is why.

amountCents.description: The FULL shared amount — what left somebody's account.

archivedAt.description:
Set when the expense vanished from KitchenOwl. Kept rather than deleted,
because the row may carry a link the user confirmed by hand.

ownShareCents.description:
The user's slice of it. These two are the most confusable pair of numbers in
the feature and are never summed with each other or with a booking.

sumAmountCents.description:
Sums for the current filter. Both are reported, always, because showing only
one of them is how the two get confused.

basis.description:
`fullAmount` | `ownShare` | `fullAmountNear` | `ownShareNear` — so the UI can
say why rather than showing a bare number.

balanceCents.description:
From `member[].expense_balance`, the only balance KitchenOwl exposes.
Negative means the user owes the household.

stale.description:
Older than `KITCHENOWL_METADATA_STALE_SECONDS`. Served anyway: a push
dialogue that will not open because KitchenOwl is down is worse than one
that opens with yesterday's member list and says so.

KoMonthlySeries.description: One KitchenOwl category or one recurring name across twelve months.

averagePerActiveMonthCents.description: Divided by the months that hold THIS subject, never by twelve.

KoOverYears.description: The household mirror, one column per year.

excludedCount.description: Kept out by KitchenOwl itself, and therefore out of every figure here.

KoOverYearsSeries.description:
One household subject — a KitchenOwl category or a member who paid — across
every year the mirror covers.

Two figures per year, never added to each other: what the household spent, and
the slice of it the user carries. For a payer the second is meaningless (they
fronted the whole amount) and is zero.

KoPayerShare.description: Who paid, which only a shared ledger can ask.

monthlyAmountCents.description:
Twelve slots, Januar first. The flow diagram shows one month at a time and
the year total alone cannot answer "who fronted June".

lastError.description:
Kept in every state. A queue item that failed silently is a booking the user
believes is in KitchenOwl and is not.

amountCents.description: Defaults to the booking's own amount, untouched.

koCategoryId.description: KitchenOwl's own taxonomy. Never derived from the app's category.

factor.description: Integer weight. `1` each is an even split; `{12, 7}` occurs in the real data.

monthName.description: German month name; data, not chrome.

KoSeriesSubject.description: A name worth charting, as the picker offers it.

KoSettlement.description:
Settling up with the household — the one place the two ledgers touch.

A settlement is money paid to, or received from, ANOTHER PERSON: it leaves the
account for good, so it is an `expense` or an `income` and it moves the balance.
It is not a `transfer` — that models money moving between the user's own
accounts, where `net_cents` is 0 by construction. See the module documentation on
`kitchenowl::settle` for why the original transfer modelling had the
double-counting argument backwards.

alreadySettled.description:
True once this period carries a settlement booking, so the button is offered
exactly once.

amountCents.description: Always positive: the sum that would change hands. `0` when settled.

balanceCents.description:
KitchenOwl's own signed balance, passed through UNFLIPPED: negative means
the user owes the household. `null` when the mirror holds no member row for
the user yet.

oneOf.description:
The settlement booking, when one exists. A personal-ledger figure, never
added to any KitchenOwl figure above it.

categoryId.description:
Where it would land — `Haushaltsausgleich`, which is where the user's own
thirteen historical settlements live.

categoryIsFallback.description:
True when that category does not exist here, so the rule table decides and
the booking may come out uncategorised. Said out loud rather than discovered.

direction.description:
`i_owe` | `household_owes_me` | `settled` | `unknown`. The word the UI reads
out, decided here so that the figure and the sentence beside it cannot
disagree — they have done exactly that once already.

oneOf.description:
What settling would book: `expense` when the user owes, `income` when the
household does, `null` when there is nothing to settle. NEVER `transfer` —
this money goes to another person, so it moves the balance.

settledBalanceCents.description:
The balance that settlement was based on, which is not necessarily today's:
expenses booked afterwards move the balance again.

suggestedComment.description: `Ausgleich <Monat>` — the spelling the spreadsheet used. Data, not chrome.

factor.description:
An integer WEIGHT, not a percentage: the share is
`amount * factor / sum(factors)`, allocated by largest remainder so the
shares sum to the amount exactly.

configured.description: The server has a URL and a token.

enabled.description:
This account opted in by running a sync at least once. The credentials are
process-global, so mirroring into every account would copy one household
into other people's books.

pollSeconds.description:
`0` means the periodic pull is disabled and only "jetzt synchronisieren"
moves anything.

reachable.description:
Derived from the last sync run, never from a live probe — this endpoint must
not block on HTTP.

KoSummary.description:
The dashboard widget. Reads the **local mirror only** and never blocks on HTTP,
so KitchenOwl being down costs a staleness warning rather than a spinner.

monthAmountCents.description:
The household's spend this month, and the user's share of it. Two figures,
always both, never added to anything from the personal ledger.

error.description: Set when the run could not finish. The rest of the app keeps working.

KoTagRequest.description: Assigns one KitchenOwl category. Exactly one of `name` or `expenseIds`.

expenseIds.description: Or an explicit set, when the user picked rows rather than a whole name.

limit.description:
How many expenses this call may WRITE before returning. KitchenOwl takes
about two seconds per update, so a name with sixteen of them is half a
minute of a request that shows nothing and dies if the browser gives up or
the page is reloaded — which is exactly what happened the first time this
ran. The caller asks for a few at a time and comes back for the rest;
`remaining` says how many that is. Defaults to 8, capped at 25.

name.description: Every untagged expense whose folded name matches, across all years.

KoTagResult.description: What actually happened, per expense where it did not.

failures.description:
One entry per expense KitchenOwl refused. The mirror still says untagged for
each of these — a mirror claiming a category KitchenOwl never accepted is
worse than an untagged one.

remaining.description:
Still untagged under this selection after the batch. Zero means done; more
than zero means call again with the same body. Failures are not counted
here — they stay untagged but calling again would only fail again.

skipped.description:
Already carried this category: skipped without a request, so applying twice
costs one round trip's worth of nothing.

KoTagSuggestion.description:
A suggested category and, always, where it came from.

The reason travels with the suggestion because the three sources do not deserve
equal trust, and a preselected dropdown with no explanation is how a wrong guess
becomes 39 wrong expenses.

source.description:
`override` — a standing correction the user gave by hand.
`precedent` — this same name already carries that category in the mirror,
`timesSeen` times. The user's own past decision, and the strongest signal.
`rule` — the personal rule table maps the name to a finance category that is
itself mapped to a KitchenOwl category.

KoTrailingCategory.description: One category over a trailing window, its twelve values in window order.

KoTrailingMonth.description: One month of a trailing window, in window order.

KoTrailingWindow.description: Twelve months ending wherever asked, ignoring the year boundary.

KoUntaggedGroup.description:
One untagged name, with everything needed to decide it in one look.

The queue is grouped by NAME rather than listed per expense because the decision
is per name: sixteen Kaufland receipts are one judgement, not sixteen. 173
expenses collapse to about 100 names, and the frequent names carry most of the
money.

amountCents.description: Both figures, as everywhere in this module, and never added together.

matchKey.description: The folded key the group was built on, and what `apply` matches against.

name.description:
The most recent spelling. Grouping folds case and trims, because two people
type these by hand.

KoYearComparison.description: The household's year against the one before it.

comparableMonths.description: The months both years actually carry expenses in.

fullyComparable.description:
False when the two years cover different months, which is when the raw
totals stop being a comparison.

years.description: Every year the mirror holds, newest first — the picker's options.

templateIds.description:
Restricts the run to a subset — the month checklist's individual ticks.
Omitted means every template due in that month.

skippedReason.description: Set when nothing was created. `alreadyBooked` is the normal, expected case.

deltaCents.description:
Non-zero when the block's own saldo marker disagrees with its rows. Recorded,
never silently adjusted.

cumulativeCents.description:
`null` for months with no bookings — the sheet's `NA()`. Zero-filling would
draw a cliff in the cumulative chart that does not exist.

MonthlySeries.description:
A single subject's twelve months — one category, or one comment.

The spreadsheet's `Filter` tab did exactly this and it is the question a
household actually asks: not "what did Auto & Parken cost" but "how much do I
spend on tanken, and is it getting worse".

averagePerActiveMonthCents.description:
Divided by the months that carry a booking for THIS subject, not by twelve
and not by the year's months — an expense that only happens in summer
should not look small.

mode.description: `category` or `comment` — which kind of subject was asked for.

months.description:
Twelve entries, Januar first. Gross legs and the net, so the UI can show
the netting rather than assert it.

subject.description: The category name or the comment, verbatim. Data, so never translated.

OverYears.description: The whole ledger, one column per year.

balancePerYearCents.description: Income minus expense, per year: the flow convention, positive is a surplus.

monthsPerYear.description:
Months with at least one booking, per year. A part year compared with a full
one is the single way this screen could mislead, so the count travels with
the figures.

OverYearsSeries.description:
One subject — a category or a type — across every year the ledger covers.

`per_year` is aligned with [`OverYears::years`] by index, and a year the
subject had no activity in is a zero rather than a hole: the row is a time
series, and a gap in the middle of one is read as "no data", which is a
different claim from "nothing was spent".

perYearCents.description: Stored expense-positive convention, like every other net in the app.

yearsActive.description:
How many of the years carry any booking at all, so "5.000 € over ten years"
and "5.000 € in one" can be told apart without reading the row.

Period.description:
A year/month pair on the wire. `period_ord` is an internal encoding —
`year*12 + month - 1` — and leaking it into the API would force every client to
reimplement the arithmetic to show a month name.

filename.description: The user's own filename, kept as metadata only. It is never a path component.

amountIsEstimate.description:
The amount varies month to month — a membership billed differently in
different months — so materialising must produce a **draft** the user
confirms with the real figure.

anchor.description: The month the cycle is measured from; due months are `anchor + n*interval`.

categoryFromRule.description:
True when the name above comes from the rule table rather than from an
override — so a rule change will move it, and that is worth saying.

categoryName.description:
The category this template books into: the override if it has one, otherwise
the one the rule table gives its comment. An empty cell in the list read as
"uncategorised", which was never true.

dueInPeriod.description:
Whether the template falls due in the period the request asked about, and
whether a booking for it already exists there. Both are `null` when the
request named no period.

oneOf.description:
Defaults to `active_from`, which is what makes a plain monthly template a
two-field affair.

categoryId.description:
A manual override, exactly as on a booking. Omit to let the rule table decide
at materialisation time, so a rule change still reaches future bookings.

ruleLinksDowngraded.description:
Bookings whose export said `rule` but whose rule is absent from the document.
They are restored as manual overrides so the figure never moves; the count
makes that visible instead of silent.

oneOf.description:
How `to ING` and `from Volksbank` become transfers: an ordinary editable rule,
not a hard-coded list.

SearchComment.description:
A distinct comment the search matched, with how often it occurs.

Hand-typed comments drift — `Kaufland`, `kaufland`, `Kaufland Berlin` — and a
search for one of them should say which spellings it actually caught.

comment.description: The spelling used most recently, which is the one worth showing.

byYear.description: Newest year first, and only years that actually matched.

query.description: Echoed back, trimmed, so the UI never has to guess what was asked.

SearchYearSummary.description:
One year's worth of whatever a search matched.

The point of a cross-year search is not the list — it is this: what a merchant
has cost per year since 2023, on one screen, without four page loads.

netCents.description: Stored convention: expenses minus income, so a year that earned is negative.

SeriesSubject.description: What the picker offers: every comment that actually occurs, most used first.

SettleRequest.description:
The optional body of a `POST`. Everything in it has a sensible default, which is
why the body itself is optional.

provider.description:
Which provider the login page should render for. Lets the frontend stay
ignorant of whether local auth or OIDC is configured.

SinkingFund.description:
A known annual or quarterly lump, stated once so it can be accrued monthly.

A fund books nothing. It is an EXPECTATION, compared against the ordinary
bookings in its category — a fund that created bookings would double-count the
very spending it exists to anticipate.

categoryId.description:
Optional: a fund can be a plain reminder before the user decides which
category it belongs to. Without one there is nothing to compare against, and
`spentCents` stays 0 rather than guessing.

dueMonth.description: 1..12 — the month the bill actually arrives.

StatementPayee.description: One remembered payee: the bank's spelling, and the name a person gave it.

hits.description: How often this rename has been applied or reconfirmed.

payee.description: As the bank writes it. Ground-truth data, never translated or tidied.

clearCategory.description:
`true` clears the category rather than leaving it where it is — `null` in
`categoryId` cannot say "remove it", since an omitted field is also null.

"No category", said explicitly. `categoryId: null` cannot say it, because
an omitted field is null too and must leave the category alone.

decision.description: `accepted` or `rejected`; omitted leaves the decision where it is.

rememberPayee.description: Remember what this payee is called, for every future statement.

StatementRowView.description: One staged statement line, as the review screen sees it.

categorySource.description: Where that category came from: `rule`, `suggestion`, `manual`, or none.

comment.description:
What the comment will be. Starts as a suggestion from the payee and is the
field the review exists to correct.

duplicateBookingId.description: The booking this line looks like it already is.

TrailingCategory.description: One category over a trailing window, with its twelve values in window order.

monthlyNetCents.description: Twelve entries, oldest first, aligned with `months`.

TrailingMonth.description:
One month inside a trailing window. Carries its year, because the window crosses
the year boundary and a bare "Januar" would be ambiguous in exactly the place this
view exists to look at.

TrailingWindow.description:
Twelve months ending at a given period, whatever years they fall in.

A calendar year is an accounting convention, not a unit of behaviour: in January
the year-to-date view has one month in it. This is the window that always has
twelve, which is what makes a trend visible.

fromYear.description: The first month of the window, which is eleven months before the last.

openingSource.description:
`configured` for 2026 (40.000,00 entered by hand) versus `derived` from the
previous year's close.

YearComparison.description:
A year against its predecessor.

The trap this endpoint exists to avoid: 2026 holds nine months and 2025 holds
twelve, so the raw totals make this year look thrifty by three months' worth of
spending. Every figure therefore comes twice — as it stands, and restricted to
`comparableMonths`, the months both years actually have — and the UI leads with
the restricted pair whenever the two years differ in length.

comparableMonths.description: Month numbers 1..12 that BOTH years carry bookings in, ascending.

fullyComparable.description:
True when the two years cover the same months, so the raw figures are already
a fair comparison.

previousYearHasData.description:
Empty when the previous year holds nothing at all — the UI then says so
rather than rendering a table of "+100 %".
